title: Reconnaissance
text: The adversary is trying to gather information they can use to plan future operations. Tactics include scanning networks, gathering victim host and identity information.

title: Active Scanning
text: Adversaries may execute active reconnaissance scans to gather information that can be used during targeting. Scanning may include probing victim infrastructure via network traffic or collecting data from search engines.

title: Gather Victim Host Information
text: Adversaries may gather information about the victim's hosts that can be used during targeting. Information about hosts may include hardware, software, firmware, or configuration details.

title: Gather Victim Identity Information
text: Adversaries may gather information about the victim's identity that can be used during targeting. Identity information may include names, email addresses, credentials, employee information, or other personal data.

title: Initial Access
text: The adversary is trying to get into your network. Initial access tactics include exploiting public-facing applications, phishing, external remote services, and valid accounts.

title: Exploit Public-Facing Application
text: Adversaries may attempt to take advantage of a weakness in an Internet-facing computer or program using software, data, or commands in order to cause unintended or unanticipated behavior.

title: Phishing
text: Adversaries may send phishing messages to gain access to victim systems. Phishing can be targeted (spearphishing) or non-targeted, using various delivery mechanisms.

title: External Remote Services
text: Adversaries may leverage external-facing remote services to initially access and/or persist within a network. Remote services such as VPNs, Citrix, and other access mechanisms allow users to connect to internal enterprise network resources from external locations.

title: Valid Accounts
text: Adversaries may obtain and abuse credentials of existing accounts as a means of gaining Initial Access, Persistence, Privilege Escalation, or Defense Evasion.

title: Execution
text: The adversary is trying to run malicious code. Execution tactics involve command and scripting interpreters, exploitation for client execution, and other methods.

title: Command and Scripting Interpreter
text: Adversaries may abuse command and script interpreters to execute commands, scripts, or binaries. These interfaces and languages provide ways of interacting with computer systems.

title: Exploitation for Client Execution
text: Adversaries may exploit software vulnerabilities in client applications to execute code. Vulnerabilities can exist in software due to unsecure coding practices.

title: Persistence
text: The adversary is trying to maintain their foothold. Persistence techniques include creating accounts, autostart execution, scheduled tasks, and more.

title: Create Account
text: Adversaries may create an account to maintain access to victim systems. With a sufficient level of access, creating such accounts may be used to establish secondary credentialed access.

title: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution
text: Adversaries may configure system settings to automatically execute a program during system boot or logon. Settings may also be modified for persistence.

title: Scheduled Task/Job
text: Adversaries may abuse task scheduling functionality to facilitate initial or recurring execution of malicious code.

title: Defense Evasion
text: The adversary is trying to avoid being detected. Defense evasion techniques include indicator removal, obfuscated files, masquerading, and more.

title: Indicator Removal
text: Adversaries may delete or modify artifacts generated within systems to remove evidence of their presence or hinder defenses.

title: Obfuscated Files or Information
text: Adversaries may attempt to make an executable or file difficult to discover or analyze by encrypting, encoding, or otherwise obfuscating its contents on the system or in transit.

title: Masquerading
text: Adversaries may attempt to manipulate features of their artifacts to make them appear legitimate or benign to users and/or security tools.

title: Credential Access
text: The adversary is trying to steal account names and passwords. Credential access techniques include OS credential dumping, brute force, and adversary-in-the-middle.

title: OS Credential Dumping
text: Adversaries may attempt to dump credentials to obtain account login and credential material, such as hash dumps and Kerber tickets.

title: Brute Force
text: Adversaries may use brute force techniques to gain access to accounts when passwords are unknown or when password hashes are obtained.

title: Adversary-in-the-Middle
text: Adversaries may attempt to position themselves between two or more networked devices to support follow-on behaviors such as Network Sniffing or Transmitted Data Manipulation.

title: Discovery
text: The adversary is trying to figure out your environment. Discovery techniques include account discovery, system information discovery, and enumeration.

title: Account Discovery
text: Adversaries may attempt to get a listing of accounts on a system or within an environment. This information can help adversaries determine which accounts exist.

title: System Information Discovery
text: An adversary may attempt to get detailed information about the operating system and hardware, including version, patches, hotfixes, service packs, and architecture.

title: Lateral Movement
text: The adversary is trying to move through your environment. Lateral movement techniques include remote services and lateral tool transfer.

title: Remote Services
text: Adversaries may use Valid Accounts to log into a service specifically designed to accept remote connections, such as telnet, SSH, and VNC.

title: Lateral Tool Transfer
text: Adversaries may transfer tools or other files between systems in a compromised environment. Files may be copied from one system to another to stage adversary tools or additional files.

title: Collection
text: The adversary is trying to gather data of interest. Collection techniques include gathering data from local systems and network shares.

title: Data from Local System
text: Adversaries may search local system sources to find files of interest or sensitive information prior to Exfiltration.

title: Data from Network Shared Drive
text: Adversaries may search network shares on computers they have compromised to find files of interest.

title: Command and Control
text: The adversary is trying to communicate with compromised systems. C2 techniques include application layer protocols and ingress tool transfer.

title: Application Layer Protocol
text: Adversaries may communicate using OSI application layer protocols to avoid detection/network filtering by blending in with existing traffic.

title: Ingress Tool Transfer
text: Adversaries may transfer tools or other files from an external system into a compromised environment. Files may be copied from an external adversary controlled system through the command and control channel.

title: Impact
text: The adversary is trying to manipulate, interrupt, or destroy your systems and data. Impact techniques include data encryption and data destruction.

title: Data Encrypted for Impact
text: Adversaries may encrypt data on target systems or on large numbers of systems in a network to interrupt availability to system and network resources (ransomware).

title: Data Destruction
text: Adversaries may destroy data and files on specific systems or in large numbers on a network to interrupt availability to systems, services, and network resources.
